title: The Inheritance Cliff
synopsis: Examines how parental wealth has become the primary determinant of home ownership in Australia, arguing we have constructed a de facto aristocracy while maintaining democratic forms.

content:
I want to pose a question I suspect many Australians have felt and few have said plainly: at what point does a democracy become an aristocracy in practice while keeping all its democratic forms?

The question came to me reading about a young couple who'd bought their first home in Sydney. The article framed it as a success story, a testament to discipline and sacrifice. Buried in the fourth paragraph was the detail that actually mattered - a 400,000 dollar gift from parents for the deposit - presented as unremarkable and almost incidental. I found myself sitting with that assumption for a long time.

We've developed, without quite admitting it, a two-track system. On one track are people whose parents accumulated property during the great inflation of Australian housing, and who can now transfer that value to their children as gifts, guarantor arrangements, or eventually inheritance. On the other are people whose parents didn't or couldn't. For the second group the mathematics of home ownership through wages alone have become essentially impossible.

The numbers are stark. Median Sydney house prices now exceed fourteen times median income, where in the 1980s the ratio sat closer to four. A young person on a median wage, saving diligently, would need decades to accumulate a deposit, during which prices would rise faster than the savings. The target recedes as you approach it. What we're looking at is a structural change in who can access property and how, and it will outlast any market cycle.

The Bank of Mum and Dad has become, by some estimates, the ninth largest lender in the Australian property market. Financial commentary reports this as a neutral feature of the landscape, and it's worth stopping to consider what it represents. We've outsourced a core economic function - the allocation of housing - to the accident of birth. Access to shelter, to security, to the primary wealth-building mechanism available to ordinary Australians now depends substantially on who your parents happen to be.

**Where I'm Standing**

I want to be careful, because there's a version of this argument that blames individual parents and it's wrong.

Parents helping their children isn't morally suspect. It's natural and largely admirable that people want their children to thrive, and if I accumulate resources in my lifetime I'll certainly hope to pass advantages to Arthur. I'd call that honesty about the forces that actually shape behaviour rather than hypocrisy.

The problem is a system that has made those transfers necessary for participation in basic economic life. When parental wealth becomes the primary determinant of whether someone can own a home, we've built something closer to feudalism than to meritocracy. The estate passes down. Those outside the landed families stay outside.

I should also say where I'm standing. I come from an upper middle class family. I haven't received an inheritance, and my starting position was not neutral - the stability, the education, the social capital that flows from that background are themselves inherited advantages even without a financial transfer. I mention it because honesty about one's own position seems necessary here, and it would be easy and dishonest to write as though I were observing all this from nowhere.

What strikes me most is how this intersects with everything else that's moving. Artificial intelligence is restructuring the labour market in ways that will make wage-based accumulation harder still for anyone without existing capital, and the jobs that once provided a path to property - stable professional roles with predictable advancement - are precisely the ones now facing disruption. A young person without parental support has to navigate an impossible housing market and a labour market undergoing its largest transformation in a century, simultaneously.

**A Different Principle**

The conventional responses feel inadequate to the scale of it. First home buyer grants inflate prices and transfer public money to existing owners. Negative gearing and capital gains concessions keep favouring people who already hold assets. Zoning reform is necessary and operates on timescales that offer nothing to someone trying to establish themselves now. We tinker at the margins while the divide widens.

I find myself thinking about Norway. When they found oil in 1969 they made a choice that still reverberates - rather than letting resource wealth flow primarily to private interests, they built the Government Pension Fund Global. It holds roughly 1.7 trillion dollars today, about 300,000 dollars for every citizen, and its returns finance public investment while the country maintains some of the highest living standards on earth.

We have comparable natural wealth: uranium, coal, gas, iron ore, lithium, rare earths, and agricultural capacity that could feed much of Asia. We've chosen, consistently and deliberately, to privatise the gains and socialise the costs. Our sovereign wealth fund holds around 230 billion dollars, about 8,800 dollars per Australian.

The Norwegian model rests on a principle worth stating directly: natural resources are the common inheritance of everyone, so their value should be captured for the public rather than flowing disproportionately to whoever extracts them. That isn't socialism. It's a recognition that some forms of wealth aren't created by individual effort and therefore have a different moral status from wealth that is.

I believe, perhaps unfashionably, that governments should be reluctant to tax the fruits of individual and family effort. There's something genuinely troubling about a system that taxes wages earned through labour, businesses built through risk, and savings accumulated through discipline, while allowing the unearned increment of resource extraction to flow largely untaxed into private hands. We have the incentives precisely backwards, and we've had them backwards for fifty years.

Imagine an Australia that had captured even a fraction of the resource wealth extracted since 1970. The housing affordability crisis wouldn't exist in its current form. Public infrastructure wouldn't be crumbling. The energy transition could be funded without austerity. And the inheritance cliff would matter far less, because the baseline conditions of life would be more secure for everyone regardless of who their parents were.

That ship has largely sailed and the resources extracted during the boom years are gone. The principle still applies to what comes next, because we still hold extraordinary endowments. The only question is whether we keep privatising their value or start capturing some of it.

The inheritance cliff isn't finally a housing problem. It's a symptom of a choice we've made about what kind of society this is - one that taxes labour while subsidising asset ownership, that lets the accident of birth determine access to security, that holds abundant natural wealth and distributes it in ways that entrench inequality rather than dissolve it.

Arthur will grow up in whatever society those choices produce. On current trends his prospects will depend substantially on what his mother and I can accumulate and hand him. If we manage to buy property and build some capital, he'll have a foundation. If we don't, he'll face the same cliff as everyone else, with the added complication of an economy being reshaped by AI in ways that make wage-based accumulation harder again.

I don't want my son's future to depend on winning a generational lottery, and I don't want anyone else's child to depend on losing one. The cliff is already here. What remains open is whether we say so, and what we decide to do about it.
